composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.9C (wt.%). Measured by wet chemical analysis and emission spectroscopy: Mn 28.3 ± 0.4 wt.%, Al 9.0 ± 0.05 wt.%, C 0.9 ± 0.01 wt.%, Ni not added/not detected ("–"), Fe balance. High Mn and C are used to stabilize the austenite phase at room temperature, while ~9 wt.% Al is added mainly to reduce physical density (Al acts as a ferrite stabilizer). Unlike the two companion alloys (28Mn5Ni, 15Mn5Ni), this grade contains no Ni, so no Ni-rich ordered B2 intermetallic can form and the alloy remains single-phase austenitic in the HR condition. Because it is Ni-free, this composition is the reference for assessing how Ni addition (via Ni-rich B2 precipitation) changes precipitation and recrystallization behaviour.
conclusions: 28Mn0Ni is the Ni-free, single-phase austenitic (B2-free) low-density steel used as the reference material of the study. In the HR condition, obtained by VIM melting, homogenizing at 1423 K for 2.5 h and hot rolling at 1323 K to ~13 mm, it has equiaxed γ grains of ~5–7 μm, nearly random texture, the highest twin fraction and the lowest κ-carbide fraction of the three alloys, and a bulk hardness of ~256 ± 5 VHN. Its absence of Ni (and therefore of prior B2 phase) is the key differentiator: it recrystallizes and grain-coarsens faster than the Ni-bearing 28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni alloys after cold rolling and heat treatment, and its prior 20–70% room-temperature elongation (all three alloys) informed the decision to limit cold rolling to 50% reduction. These LDS alloys are considered potential candidates for automotive and defense applications owing to their high specific strength–ductility combinations.
mechanisms: The absence of Ni keeps 28Mn0Ni free of any prior B2 phase in the HR condition; because no B2 particles (which retard boundary migration and diffusion) are present, this Ni-free alloy recrystallizes and grain-coarsens much faster than the Ni-bearing alloys after cold rolling and heat treatment.
The high Mn and C contents stabilize the FCC austenite so that the alloy remains single-phase γ (B2-free) rather than developing the γ + B2 duplex structure seen in Ni-containing grades.

Compared with the Ni-containing grades, the higher Mn level correlates with the highest annealing-twin fraction (~28–40% Σ3 boundaries) and the lowest κ-carbide volume fraction among the three alloys in the HR state.

The high Mn content and the resulting high intrinsic stacking fault energy promote planar slip as the dominant deformation mode: when this HR austenite is subsequently cold rolled, the grains deform mainly by planar slip (parallel slip bands) with no deformation twinning or strain-induced martensite.

Processing in the two-phase region is expected to limit grain growth because precipitate particles reduce grain-boundary migration and diffusivity; this is why the B2-free 28Mn0Ni, lacking such pinning particles in the HR state, is the alloy that subsequently coarsens most readily.
microstructure: In the hot-rolled condition 28Mn0Ni is a single-phase austenitic (γ, FCC) low-density steel: it is both Ni-free and B2-free, so no second phase is resolvable. The γ-matrix consists of equiaxed grains with a nearly random texture and a grain size of ~5–7 μm, similar to the other two alloys. Annealing twins are present with a twin fraction of ~28–40% (estimated from Σ3 CSL boundaries); the higher-Mn LDS alloys, including 28Mn0Ni, contained a higher twin fraction than 15Mn5Ni. Among the three alloys, 28Mn0Ni contains the lowest volume fraction of κ-carbides (28Mn0Ni < 28Mn5Ni < 15Mn5Ni). The HR microstructures of all three alloys were reported in a previous study [21] and are used here as the starting condition for cold rolling.
processing: The alloy was prepared by the vacuum induction melting (VIM) route as a 30 kg ingot, from which the sound portion was used. The ingot was homogenized at 1423 K for 2.5 h and then hot rolled at 1323 K to a final plate thickness of about 13 mm. This condition is referred to as HR (hot rolled) and is the subject of this entry. The hot rolling details were reported elsewhere [21]. In the parent study, samples cut from the hot-rolled plate were subsequently cold rolled at room temperature to ~50% reduction in thickness (to ~6 mm sheets) in several passes (condition HR + CR), and then heat treated in the range 873–1273 K for 1 h followed by water quenching; the HR state described here is the precursor of all those later conditions.
properties: The bulk Vickers hardness of 28Mn0Ni in the HR condition is ~256 ± 5 VHN (measured per ASTM E-140-02 on an AFFRI Vickers tester under a peak load of 30 kg (~300 N) with a 15 s dwell time; averaged over ten measurements per sample; the HR value is reported in [21]). This is the lowest initial hardness among the three alloys (28Mn0Ni ~256 ± 5 < 28Mn5Ni ~268 ± 5 < 15Mn5Ni ~375 ± 6 VHN). Tensile properties of the HR condition itself were not measured in the present work; in the authors' previous study [21] the three HR LDS alloys exhibited about 20–70% total tensile elongation to failure at room temperature, with the Ni-containing 15Mn5Ni alloy showing the lowest ductility. Characterization techniques applied to this and related conditions include bulk Vickers hardness testing, orientation imaging microscopy (OIM)-EBSD on a Zeiss Supra 55 FEG-SEM with EDS and Nordley EBSD detectors (TSL-OIM software, KAM and GOS analysis, Σ3 CSL twin fraction, linear-intercept grain size), and X-ray diffraction (Rigaku, Co-Kα, 45 kV, 135 mA, ~2 mm beam) for phase identification.
summary: 28Mn0Ni (Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.9C, all in wt.%) is the Ni-free member of a family of three austenitic low-density steels (LDS) studied to probe the effect of Mn/Ni ratio on concurrent precipitation and recrystallization after cold rolling and heat treatment. This entry covers the alloy in its hot-rolled (HR) condition: a single-phase, B2-free austenitic low-density steel produced by vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1423 K for 2.5 h and hot rolling at 1323 K to a plate thickness of ~13 mm. In HR condition it serves as the Ni-free reference material against which the B2-forming 28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni alloys are compared, and as the starting condition for the 50% cold rolling of the present work.
unmapped: The HR-condition microstructures of all three LDS alloys are not original to this paper: they were first reported in the authors' previous study [21] and are reused here as the starting condition for cold rolling. The HR-condition tensile elongations of ~20–70% (with 15Mn5Ni lowest) likewise come from [21].

28Mn0Ni is described as the Ni-free, single-phase austenitic (B2-free) LDS reference material; unlike the Ni-containing alloys it contains no prior B2 phase, which is stated to be why it recrystallizes and grain-coarsens faster than the Ni-bearing alloys after cold rolling and heat treatment.

The hot-rolled plate of 28Mn0Ni (like the other two grades) could be cold rolled to 50% reduction without cracking; the 15Mn5Ni alloy cracked beyond 50% reduction, so 50% was chosen as a common reduction for comparison.
